implementation_notes: The classic C++ realization is a library rather than hand-written code: Boost.Units defines quantity<Unit,Y> as a value plus a compile-time unit, with unit systems (SI) providing the base units and dimensions, so addition, comparison and conversion are dimension-checked and the 6-feet-plus-180-pounds mistake becomes a compile error at zero runtime cost. Conversions are declared once with BOOST_UNITS_DEFINE_CONVERSION_FACTOR, and construction requires both a value and a unit - from_value() is the documented escape hatch - which is what keeps unitless numbers out of the arithmetic. For time specifically the standard library already ships the pattern as std::chrono::duration (period as std::ratio, duration_cast for conversions), so reach for Boost.Units or mp-units only when dimensions beyond time are needed.
pitfalls: A dimension mismatch produces long template errors that name MPL internals rather than the offending quantity; per-dimension type aliases keep signatures and messages readable.
Implicit conversion happens only when the reduced base units match exactly, so differently scaled units need an explicit construction instead of a silent (and wrong) assignment.
With an integer value type the conversions truncate silently - pick double or a scaled integer deliberately and say so in the type alias.

variants.name: std::chrono::duration for the time dimension
variants.implementation_notes: For time the standard library is the realization: duration<Rep,Period> stores the amount with the unit as a compile-time std::ratio, the SI literals (3s, 500ms) construct values, operator+ converts automatically to the finer period, and duration_cast makes conversion explicit at the point where precision is deliberately dropped (floor/ceil/round in C++17 for documented rounding). Prefer it whenever the quantity is a duration; do not generalise it to other dimensions, and do not hand-write another duration type next to it.
pitfalls: duration_cast truncates towards zero, so 1500 ms becomes 1 s - use floor/ceil/round when the rounding policy matters.
Mixing integral and floating-point durations changes the common_type of an expression (treat_as_floating_point); keep one representation per interface.
Only time is covered: a length or a mass still needs a general units library or a hand-written type, and stretching duration to them is a dead end.

variants.name: Hand-written quantity over std::ratio
variants.idiom_name: value type + std::ratio scale + constexpr operators
variants.implementation_notes: When no units dependency is acceptable, the smallest honest realization is a template holding the value plus a unit tag whose scale is a std::ratio: constexpr constructors, arithmetic that converts to a common unit, an explicit named conversion, and a std::hash specialization so it behaves like a number. It is std::chrono::duration generalised - the same idea with your own dimension list and conversion table in one header - and it is only worth maintaining for a small, closed set of units.
pitfalls: The unit tag must encode the dimension, not only the scale, or the conversion template will happily convert kilograms into feet.
Hand-copied conversion factors drift from the ones in the database or the device protocol; keep one table and generate or check the other side against it.
